titleEn: You have searched me and known me
progression: | Em Em | Cmaj7 Cmaj7 | Am Am | B7 Em |
intro: Twenty four verses in four blocks of six: you know me, I cannot get away from you, you built me, and then a sudden turn on the wicked before the last two verses hand the searching back to God as a request. The Hebrew is late and carries Aramaic forms, and several of its words occur nowhere else in the Bible. It is not part of the fixed daily order of prayer; it is one of the psalms people take up on their own. Watch the first verb and the last: the psalm ends by asking for exactly what it opens by stating as a fact.

stichs.en: For the leader. A psalm of David.
LORD, You have searched me and You know.

verses.summary: The claim of the whole psalm in two verbs, searched and knew, with the object suffix me attached to the first.

stichs.en: You know when I sit down and when I get up;
You make out my thought from far off.

verses.summary: Sitting and standing, the two poles of an ordinary day, stand for all of it. The last word puts distance in the sentence and the knowing crosses it anyway.

stichs.en: My going out and my lying down You have measured,
and You are familiar with all my ways.

verses.summary: Two more pairs that mean everything between them: the road and the resting place, then all my ways. The final verb is the one used for being long familiar with something.

stichs.en: There is not a word on my tongue
but You, LORD, already know all of it.

verses.summary: From actions to speech, and then further back than speech: the word is known before the tongue reaches it.

stichs.en: Behind and in front You have hemmed me in,
and You have laid Your palm on me.

verses.summary: Behind and in front is not an embrace here. The verb is what a besieging army does to a city, and the hand laid on top is pressure, not comfort.

stichs.en: Such knowledge is too wonderful for me,
too high; I cannot reach it.

verses.summary: The first movement ends in surrender, not praise. Knowledge is called too high, and the speaker says plainly that he cannot get up to it.

stichs.en: Where shall I go from Your spirit,
and where shall I flee from Your face?

verses.summary: The second movement begins as an escape plan. Spirit and face are the two ways God is present, and the question asks where either one is not.

stichs.en: If I climb to the heavens, You are there;
if I make my bed in Sheol, there You are.

glosses: and if I make my bed
verses.summary: The vertical extremes. Heaven and Sheol are as far apart as the world goes, and the answer at both ends is a single word: there.

stichs.en: Let me lift the wings of the dawn,
let me settle at the far edge of the sea.

verses.summary: The horizontal extremes, and the most beautiful line in the psalm. Wings of dawn is speed, the far edge of the sea is distance, and both are hypothetical.

stichs.en: Even there Your hand would lead me,
and Your right hand would take hold of me.

verses.summary: The escape ends with the hand that was pressing down in verse 5 doing the leading instead. Same hand, different verb.

stichs.en: And if I say: surely darkness will cover me,
then night is the light around me.

verses.summary: The last hiding place is not a location but a condition. If space will not hide him, perhaps the absence of light will.

stichs.en: Even darkness is not too dark for You,
and night shines like the day:
the dark and the light are the same.

verses.summary: Darkness is measured against God and found to be no darkness at all. The verse ends by flattening the pair rather than declaring a winner.

stichs.en: For You made my inmost parts,
You wove me together in my mother's belly.

verses.summary: The third movement, and the argument shifts from where God is to where the speaker came from. The verb for weaving is domestic, not royal.

stichs.en: I thank You that I was set apart in awesome ways;
wonderful are Your works,
and my soul knows it very well.

verses.summary: The only thanksgiving in the psalm, and it is thanks for being made strange. The word rendered wonderful is the same root as the too wonderful of verse 6.

stichs.en: My frame was not hidden from You
when I was made in secret,
embroidered in the depths of the earth.

verses.summary: Made in secret and in the depths of the earth: the womb is spoken of as a place underground, the same language the ancient world used for the grave.

stichs.en: Your eyes saw me still unformed,
and in Your book all of them were written,
days that were shaped when not one of them was there.

verses.summary: The book. Before the shape was formed the days were already written, and the last clause is the hardest in the psalm: not one of them, or one of them not yet.

stichs.en: How weighty to me are Your thoughts, O God;
how vast is the sum of them.

verses.summary: The response to all of it is not fear but arithmetic that fails. Weighty and vast are quantity words, and the counting starts here.

stichs.en: Were I to count them, they are more than sand;
I wake, and I am still with You.

verses.summary: The counting breaks down against sand. Then the verse stops being about number: whatever waking means here, the presence is there on the other side of it.

stichs.en: If only You would kill the wicked, O God;
you men of blood, get away from me.

verses.summary: The turn, and it is violent. Nothing in the first eighteen verses prepares for it, which is why the verse is so often dropped when the psalm is quoted.

stichs.en: They who speak of You with scheming,
who take up Your name in vain, Your adversaries.

verses.summary: The charge is specific: they use the name. This is not general wickedness, it is speech aimed at the God the psalm has been describing.

stichs.en: Do I not hate those who hate You, LORD,
and loathe those who rise against You?

glosses: and with those who rise against You
verses.summary: The hatred is presented as loyalty, and phrased as two rhetorical questions rather than a boast.

stichs.en: With a complete hatred I hate them;
they have become enemies to me.

verses.summary: The escalation, and the giveaway. The speaker makes God's enemies his own, which is exactly the move the next verse asks God to inspect.

stichs.en: Search me, O God, and know my heart;
test me, and know my disquieting thoughts.

verses.summary: The imperatives are the verbs of verse 1 turned into a request. Having declared whose side he is on, the speaker asks to be checked.

stichs.en: And see whether there is a way of pain in me,
and lead me in the way that has no end.

verses.summary: The last word is the one that reframes everything. A way of pain in me, then a way with no end, and the psalm that began with being known ends with being led.

pardes.body: Four movements of six verses. Knowledge in 1 to 6, presence in 7 to 12, formation in 13 to 18, and then 19 to 22 turn on the wicked before 23 and 24 close the frame. The frame is exact: {{1.4}} states that God has searched, {{23.0}} asks Him to search, and the two are the same verb with the same object suffix. Everything in between is the reason the request costs something. The speaker has spent eighteen verses saying that nothing about him is hidden, so asking to be examined is not a formality, and the four verses of hatred immediately before it are what he is handing over.

{{4.2}} is an Aramaic word for speech and one of the signs that this psalm is late. {{16.0}} occurs nowhere else in the Bible: it names something rolled up and not yet shaped, and later Hebrew keeps it for anything unformed. {{15.7}} is the verb of the embroiderer, the same root used for the woven screens of the tabernacle, so the body is made the way the sanctuary was made. {{20.5}} is the standing crux: as it is pointed it reads Your cities, and translators arrive at Your adversaries either by attaching it to a root meaning hostility or by reading a similar looking word, and neither solution is agreed. In the same verse the pair of verbs, lifting up and in vain, is the exact wording of the commandment against taking the name in vain.

Verse 16 is where the psalm was most worked over: a book in which days are written before the days exist runs straight into the question of what is decreed and what is chosen, and the ambiguity of the last clause, whether it says none of them existed yet or one of them did not, has kept the argument open. The turn at verse 19 is generally treated as a problem rather than a model, and the common reading takes 23 and 24 as the answer to it, since the man who has just declared a complete hatred immediately asks to have his heart examined, which is a confession that he does not trust his own verdict. {{24.3}} is read both as pain, a way that hurts, and as idolatry, because the same consonants spell the word for an idol.

The two directions of verse 8 are the standard vertical pair, and the point of the answer is that the descent is not somewhere outside. In the kabbalistic reading the light and the dark of verse 12 are not opposites reconciled but one thing seen from two distances, which is why the verse ends by equating them instead of saying the light wins. The book of {{16.4}} is read as the record that precedes the world it describes, and being formed in the depths of the earth in verse 15 is taken as the descent a soul makes into a body, so the middle movement is the story of coming down and the last verse asks for the way back, the way with no end.
